title: Air India 171's Preliminary Report Says the Fuel Switches Moved in 4 Seconds. A Federation of Indian Pilots EASA-Certified Level-D Simulator Says That Timeline Is Physically Impossible — and the AAIB Has Not Reconciled the Gap (22 June 2026)
narrative:
On 12 June 2025, Air India Flight 171 (Boeing 787-8 VT-ANB) crashed into a college hostel in Ahmedabad shortly after takeoff, killing 260 of the 271 people on board. On 12 July 2025, India's Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau (AAIB) issued a preliminary report whose load-bearing finding was that both engine fuel control switches transitioned from RUN to CUTOFF roughly three seconds after liftoff, with the Ram Air Turbine (RAT) recorded as generating hydraulic power by 08:08:47 UTC — eight seconds after the 08:08:39 UTC liftoff. Western media framed the finding as evidence of pilot action; India's Solicitor General told the Supreme Court on 13 November 2025 that the preliminary report does not actually blame the pilots. The AAIB has not released a final report.

On 19–20 June 2026 — within 24 hours of the one-year anniversary and the AAIB's interim update — the Federation of Indian Pilots (FIP), representing roughly 6,000 Indian pilots, held a press conference in Mumbai presenting results from 10 simulator tests on an EASA-certified Boeing 787 Level-D full-flight simulator under parameters matching AI 171's weight, balance, weather, and operating profile. The FIP findings directly contradict three of the AAIB's central claims.

The FIP findings: First, a manual fuel shutoff takes 10–18 seconds to trigger the sequence described in the preliminary report; the AAIB timeline of 4–5 seconds is 'physically and technically impossible' under a manual shutdown scenario. Second, the RAT, if it began supplying hydraulic power at 08:08:47 UTC, must have been triggered before total electrical failure; the AAIB's implied 'engines fail → RAT deploys' sequence is the wrong causal order. Third, the aircraft's Core Network System (Boeing 787's digital communications backbone) was one of four Category C Minimum Equipment List (MEL) items active on the aircraft as of 12 June 2025; the MEL was invoked on 9 June and remained valid until 19 June. FIP also cited CCTV from Ahmedabad airport showing the RAT deployed while the aircraft was still on the runway before rotation, before fuel cutoff could have triggered it, and the lone survivor Vishwash Kumar Ramesh's testimony of cabin lights flickering before descent began.

The challenge is not a fringe claim. Air India 787 engineers cited by The Caravan magazine's June 2026 independent investigation say the AAIB's implied relight chain — 'pilot switches to cutoff → engines go below minimum idle → pilot switches back to RUN → engines relight' — cannot be reconciled with either GE's published FADEC behavior specifications or real-world simulator behavior for the GEnx-1B engine. Their reconstruction: FADEC cuts fuel during a power disruption → FADEC attempts relight → engines go below minimum idle → pilots attempt recycle. In this chain, the pilots did not initiate the cutoff; they attempted to recover from a system-initiated event. The Free Press Journal's analysis of the Airborne Flight Recorder shows the APU (auxiliary power unit) did not come online at 08:08:45–50 UTC when the engine core was still spinning fast enough for a FADEC-commanded relight — a fact that contradicts a manual fuel cut as the originating event.

analysis:
The Air India 171 story is a documentary-credibility piece, not an OSINT satellite story. The narrative tension sits between an investigator's preliminary timeline (4 seconds from liftoff to fuel cutoff) and an EASA-certified Level-D simulator's measured behavior (10–18 seconds for a manual cutoff). FIP has produced the simulator data and submitted findings to Boeing; the AAIB has the ACARS data, the original flight recorder downloads, and the CVR transcript but has not released them. The honest journalistic frame is not 'FIP is right' — it is 'the AAIB's central causal claim is now in open conflict with a Level-D simulator, and the agency has not addressed the conflict.'

**Finding 1 — The 4-second timeline is now a numerical claim, not a measurement.** A Level-D simulator is the aviation industry's gold standard for reproducing aircraft behavior under controlled conditions. If 10 simulator runs under AI 171's match parameters show a manual fuel shutoff cannot trigger the AAIB sequence in 4 seconds, the AAIB's central number becomes a claim rather than an observation — and the agency has not produced its own test protocol showing otherwise. The AAIB has not released the underlying ACARS data that would either confirm the manual-cutoff interpretation or expose it as a downstream effect of a FADEC-initiated event. The agency's refusal to publish a final report six weeks after its own minister publicly committed to one is the procedural fact that makes the gap visible.

**Finding 2 — The RAT timing inverts the AAIB's implied causal chain.** If the RAT began supplying hydraulic power at 08:08:47 UTC — eight seconds after liftoff — and the AAIB timeline places fuel cutoff at ~08:08:42 UTC, then the RAT deployed five seconds after the alleged manual cutoff. But the FIP analysis is sharper: the RAT is a passive device that deploys on hydraulic loss; it does not 'come online' like the APU. If hydraulic pressure was lost at 08:08:42 UTC and the RAT was already driving hydraulics at 08:08:47 UTC, the question is not when the RAT deployed but what already failed before the cutoff. The Boeing 787's Core Network System sits on the same electrical bus as the FADEC; a MEL-deferred CNS item active on 12 June 2025 is the structural candidate. The Caravan engineers' reconstruction puts FADEC ahead of the crew.

**Finding 3 — The CVR transcript is the single load-bearing document.** The media-recycled phrase 'did you cut off the fuel?' carries enormous weight in the public framing. The full CVR transcript would either confirm a deliberate crew action, reveal a system-fault alarm preceding the exchange, or expose the phrase as one line taken out of context. The AAIB has not released the transcript. India's Solicitor General told the Supreme Court on 13 November 2025 that the preliminary report does not actually blame the pilots — a statement that would be redundant if the CVR transcript unambiguously showed a deliberate crew action.

**Finding 4 — The MEL story is independently verifiable.** The MEL was invoked on 9 June 2025 for the Core Network System and remained valid until 19 June — three days after the AI 171 crash. Boeing publishes MEL remediation timelines for deferred CNS items; the AAIB has not released the AI 171 remediation status, the maintenance release documents, or the line maintenance records that show what Air India's engineering team certified on 9 June. The Caravan engineers' reconstruction depends on this material. The AAIB's silence on the MEL layer is consistent with the agency's preliminary report treating the cockpit crew as the unit of analysis rather than the maintenance chain.
verdict: [SIPHONED VERDICT]: On 19–20 June 2026, the Federation of Indian Pilots produced 10 Level-D simulator runs under EASA-certified match conditions showing that the AAIB's 4-second fuel-cutoff timeline for Air India 171 is 'physically and technically impossible' under a manual shutdown scenario. The AAIB has not produced a contradicting test protocol. The Caravan magazine's Air India 787 engineers say the AAIB's implied relight chain cannot be reconciled with GE's GEnx-1B FADEC behavior; the Free Press Journal's AFR analysis shows the APU did not come online at the moment the AAIB's timeline would require. Three documents would settle the question — the full ACARS maintenance log, the CVR transcript, and the Boeing MEL remediation timeline for the Core Network System item deferred on 9 June 2025 — and the AAIB has released none of them. India's Solicitor General told the Supreme Court on 13 November 2025 that the preliminary report does not actually blame the pilots; the agency's six-week silence on its own minister's public commitment to publish a final report is the procedural fact that converts the FIP challenge from a domain-practitioner critique into a documented evidence asymmetry. The AAIB's central causal claim ('pilot moved the switches') is now in open conflict with an EASA-certified Level-D simulator, and the agency has not addressed the conflict.
